newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Tame German data boost stable rate outlook.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tame German data boost stable rate outlook.

text.p: Calming signals emerged on the German economy on Wednesday as key economic data indicated modest growth coupled with minimal inflation, supporting the case for stable interest rates.

Growth in M3 money supply, the Bundesbank's top indicator which had surged to an alarming 11.7 percent in January, slowed to 9.1 percent in February as strong bond markets tempted investors to move funds into long-term investments.

The closely-watched west German Ifo business climate index also edged up to 93.6 in February from 93.3 the previous month, providing more evidence that the gloom that has long plagued the German corporate world is slowly lifting.
With bond and stock markets already buoyed modestly by the news, Chancellor Helmut Kohl weighed in to reaffirm his belief that the German economy will grow 2.0 to 2.5 percent this year.
"The message from all of this is that the German economy is not doing badly," said Holger Schmieding, economist at Merrill Lynch, Frankfurt.
"These figures seem to show that the economy is coming back to life," said Adolf Rosenstock, economist at IBJ Frankfurt.

Despite signs of a recovery, economists did not believe the figures would provoke the Bundesbank into making any change in interest rates in the near future and certainly not at its next policy-making meeting on Thursday.

As Germany battles with record post-World War Two unemployment, growth is still seen as far too restrained to sustain a rate increase. On the other, money supply growth remains too robust to justify easing rates.
"All in all I don't see a change (in rates) for the time being, unless there is a huge spike upward in the dollar, which might make a tightening necessary," said Schmieding.

German headline rates -- the discount and the Lombard -- have been on hold since April 1996, when the Bundesbank cut both by 50 basis points to 2.50 percent and 4.50 percent. The money market rate, or repo, was cut to 3.00 percent in August.

Economists said the sharp slowdown in M3 expansion in February raised the prospect that the indicator will fall to within the Bundesbank's target range of 3.5 to 6.5 percent this year. M3 consistently overshot Bundesbank targets throughout last year.
However, Karen Kricks-Brunnlieb, economist at Trinkaus Capital Management, warned: "An entry into the target corridor should not be expected before the summer, at earliest."

"Against this background, the Bundesbank has definitely no reason to lower its interest rates...The Bundesbank should stick to the fixed rate repo of three percent for the foreseeable future," she added.

Looking more closely at the M3 data, economists were most impressed by the stong expansion in February of money capital formation, which measures the shift into long term investments from short-term deposits and thus indicates investor willingness to tie up capital.
The Bundesbank said annualised six-month growth in money capital formation rose to 5.1 percent in February from 4.3 percent the month before, helping to depress growth in money supply.
M3 growth was also dampened by an outflow of funds in foreign transactions by domestic non-banks and by a slowdown in bank lending to the public sector which was very high in January.

But economists noted the strong pick-up in lending to companies and private individuals. Such credits rose 8.2 percent on a six-month annualised basis after 7.6 percent in January for a total volume for February of 23.3 billion marks ($13.9 billion).
The rise in the Ifo index was largely in line with expectations and seen confirming this mild recovery.
While the west German index rose, in eastern Germany, the business climate index dropped to 104.1 from 106.5 last month.
"In general this can be taken as a good sign there will be a pick-up in the economy in a moderate way," said Commerzbank economist Ann Katrin Jaenke. ($ = 1.674 German Marks)
